traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
title: Cellular Therapy: Stem Cell Transplant, CAR-T, CRS & ICANS
html:
Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy can provide disease control when other treatments have failed, but they also create distinctive emergencies. The RN must know the treatment timeline, establish a precise baseline, recognize infection and organ injury, and rapidly activate the transplant or cellular-therapy pathway when symptoms emerge. Fever, hypotension, diarrhea, rash, confusion, or rising weight may have several competing causes; pattern, timing, laboratory trends, and specialist evaluation guide the response.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate autologous from allogeneic HSCT and explain why graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs only when donor immune cells are present.
  • Recognize early infection, graft failure, GVHD, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome after transplant.
  • Identify cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) after CAR-T or related therapy.
  • Perform serial hemodynamic and neurologic assessments and safely support protocol-directed treatment.
  • Teach patients and caregivers the monitoring, proximity, driving, infection, and emergency-contact plan.

Know the therapy and the timeline

Autologous HSCT returns the patient's own collected stem cells after conditioning treatment; allogeneic HSCT uses donor cells and can provide a graft-versus-tumor effect but introduces GVHD risk. Conditioning chemotherapy, with or without radiation, causes profound marrow suppression and mucosal injury before engraftment. Track the transplant day, cell source, donor type, conditioning regimen, current immunosuppression, prophylactic medicines, central access, blood counts, organ function, and individualized infection precautions. Engraftment is assessed by sustained count recovery and clinical context; one improving neutrophil count does not eliminate infection, bleeding, or graft-function concerns.

Infection, bleeding, and graft function

Before immune recovery, fever may be the only infection sign. Follow the neutropenic-fever pathway, collect ordered cultures without delaying prescribed antibiotics, and reassess perfusion, oxygenation, mental status, urine output, and line sites. Viral and fungal risks change over time and with immunosuppression; prophylaxis and isolation practices are regimen-specific. Monitor hemoglobin and platelets, mucosal bleeding, stool or urine blood, dyspnea, fatigue, and transfusion response. Persistent or recurrent cytopenias, absent expected recovery, or falling counts after initial engraftment require prompt transplant-team review rather than an independent diagnosis of graft failure.

GVHD: donor immunity can attack the host

GVHD follows allogeneic transplant when donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Acute and chronic patterns can overlap and are no longer judged solely by a calendar cutoff. New diffuse rash, watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, or rising bilirubin can signal acute GVHD, but infection, medication toxicity, and other causes must also be evaluated. Chronic GVHD may affect skin, mouth, eyes, lungs, liver, gastrointestinal tract, joints, fascia, and genital tissues. Measure and document stool volume and character, skin distribution, oral intake, weight, hydration, liver tests, respiratory symptoms, and functional change. Do not treat diarrhea automatically with an antidiarrheal until infection, obstruction, and the transplant plan are considered. Administer prescribed immunosuppression and monitor glucose, blood pressure, infection, renal or hepatic effects, and adherence.

Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome needs early escalation

Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, also called hepatic veno-occlusive disease, can occur after conditioning injury. Rapid weight gain, fluid retention, painful hepatomegaly or right-upper-quadrant discomfort, ascites, rising bilirubin, thrombocytopenia, and renal or respiratory deterioration are concerning. Trend daily weight under consistent conditions, intake and output, abdominal findings, bilirubin, platelets, creatinine, oxygen need, and hemodynamics. Report a clustering trend early. Fluid management and disease-specific treatment are directed by the transplant team; aggressive fluid administration or diuresis without reassessment can worsen injury.

CRS: fever plus systemic inflammation

CAR-T and other immune effector therapies can trigger CRS as activated immune cells release cytokines. Fever is the defining early cue in standard grading, followed in more severe cases by hypotension and/or hypoxia. Obtain cultures and evaluate infection at the same time because sepsis can coexist and may look similar. Record exact onset relative to infusion, temperature, blood pressure and support required, oxygen need, perfusion, rhythm, urine output, and organ function. Activate the product- and institution-specific protocol. Support airway, oxygenation, and circulation; administer prescribed antimicrobials, tocilizumab, corticosteroids, or other therapies according to the specialist plan. Do not independently grade severity from fever height alone: current support needs drive grading, and fever may disappear after anticytokine treatment while toxicity continues.

ICANS: subtle language or attention change can be the first clue

ICANS can occur with CRS, after CRS improves, or independently. Establish a pre-infusion neurologic baseline and perform the ordered standardized assessment, often including the Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) score in adults. Watch for new inattention, difficulty naming objects, impaired writing, word-finding difficulty, confusion, tremor, somnolence, weakness, seizure, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. A patient who is awake but suddenly cannot write a sentence or name familiar objects may be deteriorating. Escalate immediately, institute seizure and aspiration precautions, and prepare ordered neurologic testing and protocol treatment. Tocilizumab treats CRS biology but does not reliably treat isolated ICANS; corticosteroids and other measures are specialist-directed. Exclude infection, stroke, metabolic disturbance, medication effect, and other causes rather than assuming every neurologic change is ICANS.

Discharge and caregiver readiness

Teach the exact emergency-contact plan and product-specific monitoring period. FDA labeling updates for currently approved autologous CAR-T products instruct at least two weeks of monitoring, including daily monitoring for at least one week, remaining near a qualified healthcare facility for at least two weeks, and avoiding driving for two weeks; the actual product label and treating center's instructions take priority. Patients and caregivers should report fever, breathing difficulty, dizziness, reduced urine, rash, diarrhea, jaundice, confusion, speech or writing change, weakness, or seizure immediately. Reinforce medication adherence, infection prevention, food and line safety, vaccination planning through the transplant team, and the need for long-term follow-up.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify therapy type and day, donor status, counts, fever, hemodynamics, oxygen need, neurologic baseline, skin and stool changes, weight, liver and kidney trends.
  2. Analyze cues: Consider infection alongside CRS, distinguish systemic inflammatory findings from ICANS features, and evaluate GVHD or sinusoidal obstruction patterns in context.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, hypoxia, sepsis, severe neurotoxicity, seizure, cerebral edema, major bleeding, and progressive organ injury outrank routine comfort tasks.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate the cellular-therapy or transplant pathway, obtain ordered cultures and studies, prepare respiratory and circulatory support, and implement protocol-directed therapy.
  5. Take action: Escalate immediately, perform serial standardized assessments, give prescribed treatments safely, protect against aspiration and seizure, and communicate exact trends.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm improving support needs, cognition and ICE findings, temperature and perfusion, oxygenation, organ function, counts, intake, stool, skin, weight, and caregiver understanding.

Clinical example

Three days after CAR-T infusion, a patient develops fever, hypotension, and a new oxygen requirement. The RN activates both the cellular-therapy and infection pathways, obtains ordered cultures, begins prescribed support and treatment, and documents the level of oxygen and blood-pressure support. The next morning the blood pressure improves, but the patient cannot name common objects or write a sentence. The RN recognizes that neurologic deterioration may represent ICANS even as CRS improves, initiates seizure and aspiration precautions, repeats the standardized neurologic assessment, and urgently notifies the cellular-therapy team.

Transplant precautions, antimicrobial therapy, GVHD and sinusoidal-obstruction treatment, CRS or ICANS grading, oxygen and vasopressor support, tocilizumab, corticosteroids, seizure therapy, and discharge restrictions require the specific product label, current patient data, authorized orders, local protocols, and transplant or cellular-therapy specialists.
